title: Satyavati
hook: a sage steps into a fisher girl's boat on the Yamuna, a mist comes down, and she asks for one thing
carry: think of me, and I'll come

segments.voice: Yesterday we met Satyavati, the fisherman's daughter who will one day be a queen of the Kurus — a king's daughter, a fisherman's child. Whose story of where they started did you hear? Day seven hundred seventeen.

Before the palace, there's a boat. Satyavati rows travelers across the Yamuna for her father, the chief of the fishermen. It's ordinary work, and the river is wide. One day a sage on a pilgrimage steps in and sits down. His name is Parashara. Out on the water, he looks at her, and he wants her. And the young woman holding the oar has to think fast, alone, in the middle of a river. What she says next is where today's story turns.
screen: `A FERRY ON THE YAMUNA.` → `A SAGE STEPS IN.` → `OUT ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: The Adi Parva gives Satyavati words here, and she uses them carefully. There are sages on the banks, she tells him. They can see us. So Parashara makes a mist, and the banks disappear. Then she names her next worry. I'm a maiden, she says, living under my father. What becomes of me afterward? Parashara answers that she'll remain a maiden. And then he tells her to ask for something for herself. Out of everything she could ask, she asks for one thing. Her body has carried the smell of fish since the day she was found inside one. She asks that it smell sweet instead. He grants it. From then on, the text says, people knew her by her fragrance, and it carried a long way across the land. On an island in the Yamuna, she gives birth to a son. With his mother's leave, he goes off to the forest to practice austerities. But before he goes, he leaves her a promise: whenever you think of me, I'll come. The text says he was called Dvaipayana because he was born on an island. Tradition knows him as Vyasa, the one the Mahabharata is credited to, whose disciple told it at Janamejaya's sacrifice. So hold two things from this boat. The fragrance: years from now, the scent that draws King Shantanu to a riverbank was asked for here. And the promise: think of me, and I'll come. Satyavati keeps that promise to herself for a long time. Some readers see a girl bargaining with the little power she's given. Some see a woman caught in a sage's power, asking for what she can. The text doesn't settle it. It just lets her ask.
screen: `THE BANKS ARE WATCHING.` · `A MIST COMES DOWN.` · `ONE THING, FOR HERSELF.` · `A SON BORN ON AN ISLAND.` · then, large: `THINK OF ME, AND I'LL COME.`

segments.voice: Find a steady seat and let the breath slow. Picture the river going quiet under a mist, the banks gone. Satyavati was offered one thing for herself, and she knew what it was. So try the question gently. If someone offered you one thing, not for your family, not for work, just for you, what would it be? Let the first answer come, and the second. Don't rush to the noble one. Breathe in with the question. Breathe out, and let it go quiet again. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. The ferry girl who asked for a fragrance, and kept a son's promise to herself.
Your line: think of me, and I'll come. Today, when someone offers you something, ask for the one thing you actually need. Day seven hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Vyasa is honored as a teacher in Hindu tradition, and some Hindus keep the full moon called Guru Purnima, also known as Vyasa Purnima, as a day to thank their teachers.

she named the watchers on the banks and asked what would become of her.

fork.setup: you're Satyavati. the sage tells you to ask for something for yourself. what do you ask for?
options: to be taken off the river for good.
fork.reveal: she asks for a fragrance, and that scent later draws King Shantanu to her.

original.note: Sanskrit Dvaipayana: Vyasa's name, which the text ties to his birth on an island in the Yamuna.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fisher girl with a lucky boon.
what it means: a young woman asking, in a sage's power, for one thing of her own.
what a scholar hears: the son born on that island is Vyasa, whose disciple tells this very story at Janamejaya's sacrifice.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Adivansavatarana Parva (Satyavati and Parashara on the Yamuna; the birth of Vyasa Dvaipayana)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Satyavati's objections (watching sages; her maidenhood and father), the mist, the boon of fragrance replacing the smell of fish, the island birth, and Vyasa's parting promise.
The text's explanation of the name Dvaipayana (island-born) is given as the text's, not as a lexicon etymology; confirm Ganguli states it.
The encounter raises questions of consent for modern listeners; the script describes it plainly and offers two unattributed readings without ranking. A Keeper may wish to adjust the tone.
